title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
text:
"Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard.

"It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator.

"You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS.

He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs".

"But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon.

A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather.

In April, Google said people are now translating , external one trillion words a month with Google Translate.

That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatCGT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems.

Direct sales of machine translation , external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year.

"For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages.

"For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says.

With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia.

Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI.

"Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains.

But that human input is required less and less.

"The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft.

"Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman.

Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French.

She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them.

"There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said.

The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié.

When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y".

In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase.

The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees.

Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field.

"The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations.

She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth).

"That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter.

She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult.

"Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot."

"If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon.

Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

"When you have words with different meanings, it's usually very clear for a human which one applies because they understand the context, but when a machine translator comes across the sentence 'translate into Polish', for example, it is quite capable of deciding it must be all about shoe cream, says Yvon.

Context is often crucial. If an AI translator hasn't grasped that we're talking about a football match it is liable to mis-translate "taking a corner".

Last year OKA ran a study, funded by Wikimedia. It studied 119 articles, 10 language pairs and more than 1,000 hours of translator work.

"27% of the AI-generated text still got corrected before publication. Three quarters of those corrections were errors the AI introduced, and 5 to 6% of errors changed the meaning of the original text," says Zimmerman.

Eradicating those errors is likely to be challenging.

"As things stand, I think the fundamental way these systems function makes it quite hard to imagine how they could become 100% reliable," says François Yvon.

This is because probability is a crucial part of the way AI translates each word rather than another and what is probably correct is not the same as what is correct. Especially in the realm of something as subtle and surprising as language.…

title: Lisandro Martínez hits out at Manchester United hierarchy: ‘I expect more’
author: Sid Lowe at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano
text:
Defeat to Atlético Madrid ‘reflects how our club is’

Argentinian says club has not invested enough in players

Lisandro Martínez has hit out at the Manchester United hierarchy, blaming the lack of investment as their dismal start to the season continued. Goals from Pablo Barrios and Ademola Lookman pushed United to a 2-0 defeat at Atlético Madrid, and the Argentina defender described that as a “mirror” of the way the club are. “Tonight it is easy to say the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas,” he said, pointing upwards.

Asked for his appraisal of the night, Martínez said: “Really poor, really poor. I have to control myself a lot but sometimes is a reflection of the mirror of how is our club at the moment.

It is annoying, disappointing coming here and I am not seeing my team trying to get an amazing result here.

“I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night. Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team.”

United won 12 of 17 games under Michael Carrick last season but during the summer they made only three major signings – Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans – plus the back-up goalkeeper Karl Darlow on a free transfer from Leeds, and have won only twice in all competitions so far this term. They have suffered the worst start to a league campaign in 40 years.

Asked if the manager had been backed sufficiently, Martínez replied: “I don’t think so. He does his best. Every season is different. You can’t stay with what you did last season. The teams knows how you play, they know every detail, if you don’t change next season [it] is a big problem.

“You can’t keep changing, changing, changing the manager. What about other areas?” Martínez added, looking up. “I can’t say more.”

When Martínez’s words were put to Carrick, he said: “I haven’t seen the interview. I have half-heard about it. I think it’s a little bit the emotions of the game [talking]. I have to find out a bit more about it to be honest to decide what and if anything is going to be done. I can’t comment further.”

United’s manager also insisted that his side had “four almost one vs ones” and that he did not understand Leny Yoro’s red card on a night when they could have gone back to Manchester with a different result. “It is easy to look and think there is something deeply wrong, I understand that, but the players have been great,” he said. “There’s willing, and [they are] disappointed that they haven’t come out of here with something. We think we could have, should have.”

title: Man Utd defender Martinez issues scathing attack on board
text:
Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has launched a blistering attack on the club's hierarchy for not strengthening the squad following qualification for the Champions League.

Tuesday's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid means United have now gone five games without a win.

Their most recent victory was against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September. United's only other win in nine matches this season came against newly promoted Ipswich at Old Trafford, when they had to come from behind.

The Red Devils finished third in the Premier League last term to seal a Champions League return for the first time in three years.

They won 12 of Michael Carrick's 17 games in interim charge following the dismissal of Ruben Amorim in January, which was enough to earn the former United midfielder a permanent two-year contract as head coach .

"We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well," Martinez told Amazon Prime.

"Atletico have an amazing team and they deserved to win today.

"I expect more [investment]. 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox].

"I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.

"Tonight it is easy to [blame] the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas."

Martinez's view has been echoed by many external observers and has also been mentioned by some inside Old Trafford.

The failure to bring in striking support for Benjamin Sesko and competition at left-back for Luke Shaw have both been highlighted in a summer when United spent £155m on three midfielders to the exclusion of any other position.

Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was sitting next to United chief executive Omar Berrada in the Metropolitano Stadium on Tuesday.

They have sacked managers in the past two seasons after backing them the previous summer, with Erik ten Hag dismissed in October 2024, before Amorim was shown the exit door in January 2026.

"You can't keep changing, changing, changing the manager," said Martinez. "What about other areas? I can't say more.

"Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team."

Martinez's comments echo similar ones made by his Argentina defensive partner Cristian Romero against the Tottenham board last season.

Ironically, Romero was in Atletico's side against United after his summer move to Spain.

Martinez, meanwhile, has one year left on his United contract and has yet to agree an extension.

Former United players Wayne Rooney and Ashley Young were in Madrid for the game.

Discussing Martinez's comments on Amazon Prime, both said the defender had gone too far and the damage inside the dressing room could be significant.

"Something like that will rip that dressing room apart," said Rooney.

The former England and United captain recalled his own public criticism of the club in 2010 which drew a fierce response from boss Sir Alex Ferguson.

Rooney said it had been a mistake which he had apologised for.

"It is disrespectful to his team-mates," he said. "He is saying his team-mates aren't good enough.

"Bruno [Fernandes] is the only one with any right to say that. Behind closed doors, it happens - but that interview isn't going to help...

"[Martinez] has tried to speak on behalf of the players but done it the wrong way.

"It looks like a player trying to look after himself. It was very premeditated. It is sad because you need everyone to stick together, you need to be as one."

Tielemans - who United bought from Aston Villa for £35m in July - also spoke to the host broadcaster but opted not to respond to the question.

Commentating on the game, and speaking before Martinez, former England striker Alan Shearer said he felt Carrick had been let down.

Young feels Martinez should have kept his counsel.

"We know recruitment has to work and be better but players have to be better," he said. "They are the ones who have to produce.

"There's going to be no change now. That could create [issues] all week after what was a good performance."

Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former England keeper Paul Robinson said he could understand Martinez's point.

"I question his timing because with the noise around Manchester United at the moment, positivity needs to come out of the dressing room," he said.

"But on the flip side, I actually quite like it - a player being honest.

"Manchester United fans don't need their players coming out saying 'we're doing OK, the squad's strong enough'.

"Everyone can see they didn't recruit well enough and they need more players and the squad's not strong enough."

Although United were much improved on their tepid display against Tottenham at the weekend, conceding inside the first minute did not reflect well on Carrick.

And they have now gone five games without a win for the first time since 2024-25, when it happened under both Ten Hag and Amorim.

Carrick remains under intense pressure, although Martinez's words will bring renewed focus on Wilcox.

The former Southampton executive's appointment as football director is starting to be questioned, as are decisions taken by Ratcliffe and Berrada since the Glazer family stepped back despite remaining as majority shareholders.

In addition to sacking Ten Hag and Amorim, they also dismissed highly respected Dan Ashworth in December 2024 just five months after his appointment as sporting director.

Ratcliffe has also been blamed for increasing ticket prices and launching what the club said was a ticket touting investigation among season ticket holders, but which fans felt was an attempt to drive them out in favour of 'tourist' supporters.…

title: Barrios strikes after 53 seconds as Atlético pile misery on 10-man Manchester United
author: Sid Lowe at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano
text:
Michael Carrick had seen it in his players, he said, but no one else can. Not so far in the Premier League, where they have suffered their worst start in 40 years , and not here in Madrid, where Manchester United’s head coach insisted they would embrace the challenge. The reaction was coming, he promised; he had looked at them and was sure of it. Instead, they were a goal down after just 53 seconds and all that came was the old familiar sting, that early opener from Pablo Barrios and a second from Ademola Lookman condemning them to another defeat.

So much for a reaction, a rebellion: in their place a kind of resignation, a sense that maybe this is just United’s reality: a game that began badly, did not get very much better, and finished even worse. True, the result could have been different, Bryan Mbeumo unable to convert two first-half chances while Bruno Fernandes struck the bar and put an opportunity wide, but that did not diminish the feeling that something is really wrong. It may even have deepened it.

Even the late, harsh red card for Leny Yoro which can be offered in mitigation did not change a simple fact: at the end of another insipid night, United lost. United are lost, perhaps.

“Sometimes when it’s not quite going for you, you see who’s really there,” United’s manager said the night before, a message that perhaps hinted at something rotten beneath the surface, but on the opening goal no one was really there. They weren’t there on the left, where Lee Kang-in’s pass sent Álex Baena into a wide-open space; they weren’t there to close him down as he cut into the area; and they weren’t there on the right either, where Barrios was running through alone. Baena laid across and Barrios’s shot went off Ayden Heaven and into the net.

Barrios held up six fingers, the number of the club captain, Koke, whose mother had died in the hours before kick-off. From the bench Koke’s shirt was raised. All around the Metropolitano, supporters roared. This was set, it seemed.

Although another effort from Baena soon hit Lisandro Martínez, United did find a foothold and could have found a way back. Mbeumo had two clear chances in quick succession: the first, after nice footwork on the right, went wide; the second, following a neat exchange with Youri Tielemans, was stopped by Jan Oblak on the other side. From the corner, Carlos Baleba headed straight at the keeper.

That was short-lived, though, Atlético soon asserting themselves, moving the ball with a pace and conviction United couldn’t match. Barrios and Baena couldn’t be controlled, and the spaces they opened were vast. The pressure United applied tended to arrive late or not at all. On the touchline too the contrast was stark: Diego Simeone prowled, Carrick stood motionless in the corner of his technical area, chin in his hand. The Argentinian was booked for waving an imaginary card. Maybe United’s manager could try that. Something, anyway.

By half-time, Atlético had enjoyed 66% of possession. They could also have had a greater lead. Álex Grimaldo rattled a superb free‑kick off the bar and just before the break Johnny Cardoso’s sweeping finish was ruled out when the video assistant referee revealed a Marcos Llorente handball in the buildup. The second half then began with a neatly floated ball from Barrios setting up Julián Álvarez to volley against a post. Again, the space, time and the ease with which the move played out was just too big.

At the other end, Bruno Fernandes then had a wonderful opportunity to level it. Tielemans did superbly to find him, the ball sitting up and Oblak coming off his line to meet him – the kind of opportunity, in short, that is supposed to end only one way but that this time ended another.

United’s captain lifted the ball past the keeper and wide. Soon, Atlético were back again, Baena bending a shot wide, although Atlético appeared to have settled, the game drifting. That perhaps suited United: with Atlético’s threat no longer so present, the ball was theirs for the first time and the lead was still only one, opportunity there. Fernandes, increasingly involved, swung a shot against the bar.

Which was when it finally, definitively and far too easily fell apart. Suddenly, on 74 minutes, Jonathan David was running through the middle on to a Morten Hjulmand ball. Yoro went with him, grappling as they ran, and the pair fell. Although Glenn Nyberg didn’t give a foul, allowing the move to play out with David scrambling the ball to Lookman, a voice in his ear called him to the screen to watch the challenge again. When he returned, he had a red in his hand.

The decision felt harsh. It was also the end. Three minutes later, Atlético were running through United again. Grimaldo slotted a pass into David, inside the area and, although his shot was saved by Senne Lammens, Lookman was there to score. Heaven and Fernandes were removed; this was done, nothing left to fight for, not that they had fought much in the first place, the reaction postponed for some other day.

title: Gravel Burn introduces 'new dimension' of teams classification at October stage race while schedules revealed for BWR and Grasshopper series - Gravel Bits
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
The second edition of the seven-day Gravel Burn gravel stage race in South Africa, October 25-31, introduces a teams classification with points to determine standings and prizes. It will be the first such classification recognition at a gravel stage race.

Trade teams of three to four riders, as well as alliances of independent riders, will be eligible for the new classification. The top three riders from each team will earn points that will contribute to the daily standings.

Organisers developed the format in collaboration with several individuals, including pro road and gravel veteran Peter Stetina of Canyon x DT Swiss ATR and Adam Hansen, president of the CPA (Cyclistes Professionnels Associés), both having participated in last year’s inaugural race.

"This innovation provides another dimension to the racing and also rewards the riders’ efforts and the teams’ investment," said race founder Kevin Vermaak.

"Independent ‘privateer’ racers formed the foundation of professional gravel racing, adding to the ‘freedom’ and charm of gravel. We recognise that the emergence of ‘superteams’ is a threat to that. That’s why we opened the Teams Classification to all to help level the playing field, where they may form ad-hoc teams to compete with the more formal outfits.”

Canyon x DT Swiss ATR will field a women's team led by former Unbound Gravel 200 winner Carolin Schiff. They will also start two men's teams, one led by former US gravel champion Bradyn Lange. Scott-SRAM will have one team in each division, the women's team including Life Time Grand Prix contender Alexis Skarda and the men's team with Filippo Colombo, who won the UCI Gravel World Series Ceder race in February. Toyota Specialized Imbuko will have two men's teams with all-South African rosters, while Mattia De Marchi will lead a three-rider men's team for The Grip.

The solo race remains the foundation of Nedbank Gravel Burn, with a $150,000 US prize purse split equally between the pro women and pro men categories, including daily payouts to the top 3 and overall top 10. Gravel Burn is a full-service stage race in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, covering 750 kilometres and 8,500 metres of elevation gain.

Among the debutants for individuals are two-time Marathon MTB world champion Henrique Avancini of Brazil, multi-time Japanese XCO mountain bike champion Kohei Yamamoto, as well as 18-year road pro and a former Cape Epic winner Jakob Fuglsang.

Last year's men's champion Matt Beers returns, as well as runner-up Simon Pellaud. Women's champion Axelle Dubau-Prevot will defend her title, lining up against third-placed Hayley Preen.

Five events have been confirmed for the Belgian Waffle Ride schedule next year, with a new Colorado event taking shape. Registration opened October 13 for a quartet of US events spread from March to September, while Mexico takes place in late November.

The sequence of events remains the same, opening in Arizona in early March and then moving to Southern California on May 2, the 16th season for the signature event. The Utah event in Cedar City shifts from June to mid-May, and the Bozeman, Montana event then moves from June to mid-September.

Event organisers Monuments of Gravel are looking to fill the summer with a new event in Colorado, though the location has not been named and it is not known if this will be part of the series. The final ride in the BWR mixed-surface collection will again be held in Mexico on November 21, but is not part of the elite series.

"What began as one questionable idea in San Diego has now carried us through more than 42 events, with a remarkable collection of riders, partners and friends giving it far more life than we could have imagined," noted BWR founder Michael Marckx.

The Quad-Tripel Crown of Gravel series has been offered for several seasons across the US-based collection of events, and will return with the best three of four races determining elite winners. A usual suspect in the series has been Utah, but it may be a standalone race in 2027, according to organisers, and could become a UCI Gravel World Series qualifier.

Belgian Waffle Ride schedule 2027

September 18 - BWR Montana

The race schedule for the 2027 Grasshopper Adventure Series , now in its 30th year, was released with five races in northern California. The opener takes place at Low Gap on January 31, a 59-mile gravel event with 95% dirt tracks in Ukiah, and culminates at Ukiah Mendo Epic on May 23, a 70-mile mixed-terrain adventure in the same area.

The middle of the schedule includes the classic mixed-terrain Huffmaster on February 28, the road and climbing-heavy King Ridge on March 20 and the gravel-singletrack challenge of Jackson Forest on April 10.

Registration is open , and a series pass for all five events is $675, plus fees, with individual races at $155 each. Prices go up after November 30, two months before the opener.

Last year, Jen Tavé (SpeedBlock-Terún Pro Cycling) and Cassius Anderson (Marin Service Course) secured the overall titles for elite divisions in the five-race Grasshopper Series.

Grasshopper Adventure Series schedule 2027

January 31 - Low Gap at Ukiah, California

February 28 - Huffmaster at Maxwell, California

March 20 - King Ridge at Guerneville, California

April 10 - Jackson Forest at Casper, California

May 23 - Ukiah Mendo Epic at Ukiah, California

title: Eneco Tour: Jakob Söderqvist secures leader's jersey as fastest rider in nighttime prologue at The Hague
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) won the prologue Tuesday night in The Hague to take the first leader's jersey of the Eneco Tour .

Sweden's time trial champion was the third-to-last rider on the 3.1km course and posted a winning time of 3 minutes, 32 seconds. A surprising time just seven-tenths of a second slower gave 23-year old Wessel Mouris (Unibet Rose Rockets) second place. Last year's stage race GC winner Christophe Laporte (Visma-Lease a Bike) was third, 1.4 seconds behind the winner.

"These prologues are so much adrenaline, and you're really in a hot box in the end and super on your nerves when you cross the finish line," Söderqvist said to TV cameras at the finish.

He had no idea how tight the times were, and said "oh, better buy a lottery ticket then" when told his time was half a second better than Wessel Mouris.

"I had a pleasure to have a couple of days in orange also last year, and to be back here with good enough shape to start it even better."

For a while it looked like both Mouris brothers would grab podium spots, with Michiel Mouris (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) going second to his brother. Then the final four riders in the final wave shook the standings on scorching rides.

Great Britain's time trial champion Ethan Hayter (Soudal-QuickStep), who won the prologue last year, knocked Michiel Mouris down a spot with a faster time by 1 second. Then Laporte and Söderqvist dispatched the 19-year-old to fifth place, Hayter going fourth, and one brother on the podium.

The recreated Tour of Holland, now Eneco Tour, made a return last year after a 21-year absence from the UCI calendar, and the composition of two time trials and four road stages was replicated for the 2026 edition. However, the twist this year was that all six days of racing integrated racing for pro women, formerly the Ladies Tour of Holland. The blend of staggered start times and similar routes using circuits began with the Prologue.

The action began Tuesday with a unique process for the 3.1km prologue - waves of women and men sharing the same course. The first 28 women took the start in The Hague at one-minute intervals followed by a five-minute break and then the first 28 men hit the course with the same spacing. This pattern for alternating waves was repeated, with a total of 88 women and 88 men on the start list, the early riders seeing the sun setting while the city course became illuminated by street lamps in the darkness.

The start ramp was inside the Sportcampus Zuiderpark multi-functional arena, Robbe Claeys (Volkerwessels Cycling) the first men's rider down the ramp at 18:34 local time for a quick lap around the park, and setting the standard at 3:52.

Nils Eekhoff (Picnic PostNL) took over the hot seat just six riders later with 3:47, and then was dispatched by Joeri Schaper (Soudal-QuickStep) who went four seconds faster.

The second wave of 30 riders started with Thor Verleysen (Volkerwessels Cycling). Eight riders later, Hartthijs De Vries (Unibet Rose Rockets) flew across the course as the first rider to go under three minutes, 40 seconds, posting 3:39. He was nearly knocked off the hot seat by Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike), who came through six-tenths of a second slower.

It was De Vries' teammate Thomáš Kopecký who then took over with 3:37. He held the best time as only Pepijn Reinderink (Soudal-QuickStep) came within one second from the next six riders completing the middle wave.

The final wave saw 23-year-old Wessel Mouris grab the lead in a time of 3:33. The TV camera showed him smiling broadly when his brother, Michiel Mouris almost took the spotlight, going just two seconds slower. The brothers, however, were one-two with 15 riders to go.

The last three riders featured Söderqvist, Laporte and New Zealand TT champion Finn Fischer-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe). Söderqvist stormed around the circuit for the best time, with Laporte getting a podium spot, but Fisher-Black coming up short in sixth.

After the prologue, stage 1 takes place in Ede with a flat 40-kilometre circuit that the men tackle three times and women twice. The men's stage begins after the women's finish.

title: Eneco Tour Women: Lieke Nooijen dominates prologue for first race leader's jersey
author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
text:
Lieke Nooijen (Visma-Lease a Bike) secured the prologue victory and took the first leader's jersey at the Eneco Tour Women . The Dutch rider covered the 3.1km course with the fastest time of 3:51, beating her compatriots Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) and Lonneke Uneken (VolkerWessels) by eight seconds in The Hague.

Nooijen started her time trial in the third of three waves, surpassing both Kool, who posted the early benchmark and had sat in the hot seat since the opening wave, and Uneken to take the day's spoils.

The Dutch road race national champion now leads the overall classification heading into stage 1 in Ede on Wednesday.

"I'm super happy with this victory. I've worked really hard towards this, so it's great to win such a short prologue by eight seconds," she said.

"I went full gas from the start and managed to maintain my speed throughout. These short efforts really suit me, and that paid off today."

This year all six days of racing will integrate stages for pro women, formerly the Ladies Tour of Holland, and for pro men, formerly the NIBC Tour of Holland, with staggered start times and similar routes.

The action began Tuesday with a unique process for the 3.1km prologue - waves of women and men sharing the same course. The first 30 women took the start in The Hague at one-minute intervals, followed by a five-minute break, and then the first 30 men hit the course with the same spacing. This alternating-wave pattern repeated, with a total of 88 women and 88 men on the start list.

During the first wave of the women's prologue, Kool posted the fastest time of 3:59, averaging nearly 17kph across the 3.1km course. Femke Markus (SD Worx-Protime) and Margaux Vigié (Visma-Lease a Bike) were both three seconds slower in second and third place

However, the second wave started about thirty minutes with three riders slotting in behind Kool; Sandrine Tas (Lotto Intermarché Ladies) stormed into the runner's-up spot just a fraction of a second slower, Maud Rijnbeek (VolkerWessels) a two seconds back and Letizia Borghesi (AG Insurance-Soudal) at three seconds back, bumping Markus and Vigié out of the top three.

The third wave on course would decide the final top placings of the prologue, and while Kool was the day's leader for much of this event, her time was encroached upon by Uneken, who stormed across the finish line with the second-fastest time of the day, a fraction of a second slower than Kool.

But there would be one faster rider on course to surpass them both, with Nooijen putting a stamp on the prologue with the victory and the event's first leader's jersey.

title: A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
text:
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.

Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.

But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.

Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.

That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.

Morocco never found the finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.

For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.

The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.

At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.

The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.

But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.

"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".

"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.

"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."

Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A

From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.

He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.

And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.

Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.

The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.

President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.

Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.

"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."

Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that the project is using money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.

Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.

The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.

But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.

The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.

Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo , at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.

Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.…

title: What are 'papaya rules' in Formula 1?
text:
'Papaya rules' are a code of conduct for McLaren team-mates Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris on the racing track.

The word 'papaya' refers to the colour of the fruit that bears a resemblance to the iconic orange colour of McLaren.

The drivers are often told of 'papaya rules' on radio messages during races when they are battling each other.

It essentially reminds the drivers that they are free to race, but they must keep the battle fair, clean and avoid colliding.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said both Piastri and Norris have been involved in creating the code.

It also ensures equality and fairness between the two drivers as McLaren do not have a designated 'number one' driver.

During the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix sprint race, there was a final-lap collision between the McLarens as Norris tried to pass Piastri at Turn Five.

Piastri defended his position but the cars touched and spun in unison, ending the Australian's race while Norris went on to finish eighth.

Stella said: "Very simply, it is unacceptable that two McLarens ever come together on track. This is a fundamental principle of how we go racing, and something both drivers are very well aware of."

The guidelines caused tension between the two drivers as they fought for the drivers' championship - which was won by Norris at the final race of the 2025 season in Abu Dhabi.

McLaren won the 2025 constructors' championship with six races remaining at the Singapore Grand Prix.

McLaren have been urged by some pundits to ditch their papaya rules and reduce their interference in the title battle.

Boss Zak Brown described the code of conduct after the 2024 Italian Grand as "race him hard, race him clean, [but] don't touch".

Team principal Stella told BBC Sport in 2024 that the rules "only have to do with racing with no risks, no contact between the two McLarens and respectfully".

Stella reiterated this for the 2025 championship battle between the two McLarens.

"What's important is that the championship runs within the principles," he said.

"Racing values that we have at McLaren, and that we have created together with our drivers."

title: You Can’t Ride That Bike in the Dirt
author: Kelly Matkovich
text:
Riders moving in a dirt sector at Belgian Waffle Ride Utah. (Photo: Belgian Waffle Ride)

The road bike was supposed to stay on the road. Michael Marckx was supposed to get to school on time. Somewhere between those two expectations, a dirt shortcut presented itself.

He pointed his bike down a series of whoops and across a field, passing a group of older kids who apparently had strong opinions about where bicycles belonged. “You can’t ride that bike in the dirt,” one yelled.

“I had just done it, so the argument seemed weak,” Marckx writes in his manuscript, You Can’t Ride That Bike in the Dirt . The exchange stayed with him, along with a fascination for the battered riders and cobbled roads of Paris-Roubaix, his family’s Flemish heritage, and the waffles that followed long days of running and riding. Decades later, those ingredients found their way into a Southern California bicycle event with an unusually hospitable name.

The Belgian Waffle Ride sounded like breakfast. The course suggested someone had forgotten to mention a few things.

In 2012, riders gathered over waffles and coffee before heading into a long day of pavement, dirt, climbing and sand. They returned to food, Lost Abbey ale and stories that could only have come from spending hours trying to hold themselves and their bicycles together. The arrangement proved enduring: feed people, take them somewhere extraordinary, ask more of them than they expected, and give them a place to celebrate afterward.

In 2027, Belgian Waffle Ride enters its 16th year with events in Arizona, California, Utah, Montana and Mexico, plus another destination in development. Registration opens Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at 8 a.m. Pacific , inviting riders to start planning where next year’s stories will happen.

On the course, the appeal becomes clear somewhere around the first change of surface. A smooth stretch of pavement lets a group find its rhythm, wheels humming and conversations returning. Then the road gives way to dirt. Riders spread out, look ahead and choose their lines. Someone who was working hard to stay attached on the road suddenly looks comfortable. Someone else discovers that fitness and handling are separate subjects.

Marckx and co-founder Phil Tinstman built that uncertainty into BWR. Each surface creates possibilities, and each equipment choice carries a compromise. Fast tires have their virtues until the sand arrives. A comfortable bike on rough ground may ask more of its rider on the pavement. Pacing, fueling and the ability to adapt become as useful as a big engine.

In his manuscript, Marckx describes the original course as “an interrogation of the whole cyclist.” Over the years, that idea has become Unroad: riding that follows the character of a place across whichever surfaces make the journey interesting.

It also leaves room for different kinds of riders. Professionals may be settling the race at the front while friends farther back are helping one another through a difficult sector. A first-time participant can be discovering the pleasure of riding beyond familiar roads while an experienced racer is discovering the limits of an overly confident tire choice.

The established Waffle, Wafer and Wanna distances offer different portions of that experience. The full Waffle asks for a substantial day; the middle-distance Wafer and shorter Wanna give riders other ways to explore the terrain and challenge themselves. Each leads back to the gathering that made breakfast worth getting up for in the first place.

The 2027 journey begins in the Sonoran Desert, Arizona, March 5–6 , with the fifth annual Hell of the North Desert. Sandy washes, twisting trails and open gravel give the landscape a rhythm of its own. The desert rewards attention: carry momentum here, choose a line there, save enough for whatever comes around the next bend. Between efforts, there is the pleasure of looking up and remembering why a bicycle was worth bringing to this place. Waffle, Wafer and Wanna options let riders choose how much desert they want in their day.

By May 1–2 , the community returns to San Diego County for the 16th BWR California , the Hell of the North County. This is where the original idea took root, and the changing terrain still supplies its personality. Pavement connects sandy and rocky sectors; climbs separate groups that seemed perfectly cooperative a few minutes earlier. The course keeps asking riders to change gears in every sense of the phrase. California’s weekend also includes the Gran Roadie-Oh for those drawn to a paved adventure, with its 2027 details to follow.

Two weeks later, Cedar City, Utah, hosts BWR May 14–15 . The eighth annual event, presented by BZI, moves into May and returns riders to long gravel sectors, open high-desert views and riding at altitude. Here, the distance can unfold slowly across an enormous landscape, making restraint early in the day a useful investment. Utah is also preparing for substantial changes in 2027. A fuller announcement is coming soon; for now, the new date marks the beginning of an exciting chapter for the Hell of the South West.

There may soon be another place to point the bike. Organizers are excited about adding an event in the middle of the country, potentially in July . The location, timing and course are still coming together, with details to follow as plans are finalized.

The season then reaches Bozeman, Montana, September 17–18 , for the third Hell of the Bozone. Broad valleys, rolling ranchlands, gravel climbs and backcountry terrain give the riding a generous sense of scale. Fast stretches invite an effort; rougher ground asks riders to leave something in reserve. Moving into a late-season weekend gives participants a new reason to make a trip of it, with time to enjoy Bozeman after the bike has been leaned against something sturdy.…

title: Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
text:
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".

The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.

A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".

The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.

F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.

It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.

The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.

Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A

The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.

F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.

Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.

"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.

"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."

F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".

Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."

The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.

Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."

But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.

"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.

"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.

It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.

The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.

South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.

Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.

The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

title: Who Won and Lost Most in 2026? Pogačar Crushed Then Crashed, and Picnic Has Big Problems
author: Jim Cotton
text:
(Photo: Florian Wiegand/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Tadej Pogačar doesn’t need a full season to dominate, Picnic-PostNL needs a rescue package, and moneyball tactics pay off.

They’re some of the top takeaways from the individual and team rankings in this final week of 2026.

Il Lombardia wrapped up all the major racing on the 2026 calendar last weekend, and the individual victory and UCI points rankings are all but set.

They tell some interesting tales of haves, have-nots, breakouts and busts.

Summary tables for the peloton’s top-20 riders and all 18 WorldTour teams can be found below, with splits for victories and UCI points.

These are not expected to change significantly as the season winds down with low-key races through Europe and Asia before it comes to a full stop this Sunday.

Here are five of the most eye-catching takeaways from the end-of-year leagues.

Tadej Pogačar didn’t even need a full season to obliterate everybody this year. The 28-year-old topped the victory and UCI rankings by several bike lengths, despite his season starting late at Strade Bianche and ending abruptly on August 29.

Pogi won 22 times this year and scored eight more victories next-best rider Paul Magnier.

Super-prestige victories at the Tour de France, two WorldTour stage races, Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and Strade Bianche saw Pogačar dominate the UCI points rankings in just 45 race days.

His individual 9,000-point haul from six months matched or exceeded what four entire teams could manage all year. It was more than three times what 30 riders could pick off at poor Picnic-PostNL.

Second-place Remco Evenepoel was choking on Pogi’s exhaust, 2,000 UCI points back.

It’s almost scary to consider what Pogačar could have achieved this year.

The GOAT could have finished 2026 with more than 12,000 UCI points if a brutal crash at the Vuelta a España hadn’t denied him the red jersey and the chance to fulfill the role as favorite for the world championships, European champs, and Il Lombardia.

For context, Pogačar scored 11,655 points in his Hall of Fame 2024 season.

A very tepid take? Pogačar will top the victory and points leagues again in 2027. The only question is by how far.

UAE Emirates-XRG was the winningest team of 2026, but this was a long way from its absolute rout of 2025.

The team of Tadej Pogačar, Isaac del Toro and world champion Brandon McNulty “only” won 77 times this year. That’s a long way short of the single-season win record of 95 it set last year, and its worst return since 2023.

It’s a luxury letdown for UAE Emirates-XRG.

Despite dropping 18 wins year-on-year, it remains in its own tier of the WorldTour. The state-backed superteam towers over its rival Visma-Lease a Bike and Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, who won 51 and 42 times, respectively.

So what went “wrong” for the world’s richest, deepest team in 2026?

1. João Almeida won nothing. Zilch. The Portuguese star won 10 times last year but failed to get off the mark in his illness-riddled annus horribilis.

2. Juan Ayuso left. The Spaniard won seven times for UAE Emirates-XRG last year, despite a spicy spat with management. Those victories weren’t replaced.

3. As we wrote above, Pogačar lost the chance to bank a hatful of late-season wins after he was upended at the Vuelta.

Bettering brilliance, it’s a tough job to have.

The 2026 rankings are a brutal tale of haves and have-nots.

While UAE Emirates-XRG is miles off the front, Picnic-PostNL is so far off the pace it would need multiple sticky bottles to catch up.

Picnic-PostNL won only two times this year and collected just 2,680 points.

Of the WorldTour teams, it’s dead last in the UCI points league. Beyond that, it’s been outscored by 10 lower-tier rivals in a full UCI ranking that includes ProTeams and Conti teams.

And it could have been even worse . The disaster Dutch team was stuck on just one victory until Pavel Bittner snatched sprint victory and allowed a brief flush of pride this September at Paris-Chauny.

The bad news – Bittner, the team’s brightest prospect, is leaving for Pinarello-Q36.5.

Picnic-PostNL is facing an existential crisis right now.

The squad recently denied reports it was contemplating relegating itself to the second-tier of racing for 2027, but the writing seems to be on the wall.

Money in Sport reported in January that the team has lost €19.5m over three years. Bike sponsor Lapierre is fighting for survival. Bittner’s exit, along with the departure of former winners Fabio Jakobsen and Casper van Uden, suggests the team will be fighting for survival next year, too.

The partnering women’s team is in similar trouble. It hasn’t put a single “W” in the column all year.

Picnic-PostNL should maybe consult XDS-Astana for some tips.

The Kazakh crew punched way above its mid-tier budget to land sixth in both the victory and UCI rankings for 2026.

But how does a team without one of the peloton’s “bigs” collect 32 wins and 16,028 points?! It outperformed Lidl-Trek, Soudal Quick-Step, and Alpecin-Premier Tech, all without a Tim Merlier, a Mads Pedersen, or an MVDP.

XDS-Astana reprised its points-farming policies of 2025 with wild success in 2026.

Winningest rider Matteo Malucelli took eight of his nine victories for the year by bullying lower-tier rivals in a month of late-season racing across Asia. Likewise, Christian Scaroni gobbled top-10s in all the one-day and stage races nobody else bothered to show up to.

But to give the team its due – Guillermo Silva finished 14th in the win rankings courtesy of one of the year’s breakout seasons. When he wasn’t scoring “easy wins” at 2.pro stage races, the 24-year-old won a stage, wore the pink jersey, and finished in the top-6 four times at the Giro d’Italia.

XDS-Astana gets heat for its data-driven, distinctly unglamorous approach to rider scheduling.

It’s not pretty, but it works damn well.…

title: Why McLaren cannot fix its F1 car handling until 2027
Visma-Lease a Bike Signs Belgian Teenager With Eye on Post-Vingegaard Era
author: ahood
text:
Seff Van Kerckhove won bronze in the world time trial race in Rwanda in 2025. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Visma-Lease a Bike is already building for the post- Jonas Vingegaard era and penned one of Belgium’s most hyped young talents to a long-term deal through 2030.

Seff Van Kerckhove , 18, will join the Dutch superteam’s development squad next season, with a possible fast track to the WorldTour in the works.

Hyped as a potential grand tour talent, the 18-year-old is seen by some as the Belgian prince to Remco Evenepoel . He won 11 races across 2026, including time trials and mountain stages on the European junior racing circuit.

Visma’s development boss sounds keen to give him some breathing room as the Dutch team looks to the future .

“He has shown a strong commitment to his development, and we believe he has the mindset and qualities needed to continue progressing,” said Visma head of development Robbert de Groot. “We believe Seff has the qualities to take significant steps forward over the long term.”

Van Kerckhove missed last month’s worlds in Montréal after a driver struck him during training . Visma said he is recovering well.

He will join newly crowned U23 world champion Ashlin Barry on a development squad that is hardly short of ambition.

The move also takes him out of Decathlon’s orbit. Van Kerckhove raced for its U19 squad, but will head to Visma rather than continue along the French team’s pathway toward a possible future alongside Paul Seixas .

There is a family connection waiting for him, too. Older brother Matisse Van Kerckhove, 20, will graduate to Visma’s WorldTour roster in 2027.

“It is a great honor to join one of the biggest teams in cycling,” Van Kerckhove said. “I believe in the team’s sporting project and am convinced that it offers the ideal environment for me to continue developing and get the best out of myself.”

The signing is another move in the increasingly high-stakes scramble among the WorldTour superteams to secure cycling’s next generation before someone else does.

Riders like Evenepoel, Seixas, and Isaac del Toro have proven that young riders barely out their teens can produce huge results in the WorldTour.

Every team is scrambling to find that next diamond-in-the-rough.

Netcompany-Ineos landed Spanish junior prodigy Benjamín Noval , 18, to join its WorldTour roster in 2027. The son of the former pro of the same name dominated junior stage races, and won double gold at the Montréal junior worlds .

Netcompany-Ineos also signed Patrik Pezzo Rosola — son of Olympic mountain champion Paola Pezzo — to its junior squad for 2027.

Lorenzo Finn , 19, heads to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe’s WorldTour team in 2027 after winning the Baby Giro and Tour de l’Avenir in 2026.

Another Spanish gem in Héctor Álvarez Martínez, also 19, steps up at Lidl-Trek after two seasons on its development team, a European title, and second place at the U23 worlds.

Most of the major WorldTour teams already fund their own U23 and junior development squads. Otherwise they risk being left behind.

UAE Team Emirates Gen Z will promote Davide Stella — who suffered a brutal high-speed crash at the AlUla Tour — to the WorldTour squad in 2027.

Visma has spent the past half decade building out its development operation that’s already delivering riders who can win straight away.

Per Strand Hagenes is the latest payoff. The Norwegian joined the development squad in 2022, moved to the WorldTour in 2024, and broke through in 2026 with two victories, including Sunday’s Paris-Tours, and second at E3 Saxo Classic.

Matthew Brennan is another Visma development product who enjoyed a blowout 2026. In his second full WorldTour season, the Briton won 12 races, including Kuurne-Brussels-Kuurne and five stages at the Vuelta a España .

Finding the next Vingegaard won’t be easy. Tour de France-caliber riders are the rarest of talents .

The Dane remains under contract through 2028 and turns 30 in December. With two Tour de France titles and victories at the Giro and Vuelta, he’s been at the center of Visma’s grand tour success this entire decade.

There have been unsubstantiated rumors that Vingegaard might want to end his career at Uno-X, the Danish-Norwegian outfit that recently signed Magnus Sheffield as its first American rider .

Van Kerckhove’s signing shows that Visma is clearly thinking about what comes next, even if the team’s sponsorship future remains unconfirmed and after some high-profile backroom reshuffles .

Visma still packs 2023 Vuelta winner Sepp Kuss, Matteo Jorgenson , and rising Italian Davide Piganzoli to carry its ambitions alongside Vingegaard .

Piganzoli, 24, won five races in 2026, finished eighth leading at the Giro, and hit 14th in his Tour debut.

Visma is already moving its chess pieces to stay at the top of the game.

title: F1 signs historic 10-year Rwanda deal to host African Grand Prix
Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A
text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen dominated the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, winning the main race and the sprint.

His maximum total of 33 points from the event moved him up to fourth in the drivers' standings.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc finished the race in second and championship leader Kimi Antonelli completed the podium.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race at Marina Bay.

After the last-lap incident in the sprint race in Singapore, are 'papaya rules' finally failing at McLaren, and with them the premise of running two number one drivers? - Alexandros

The crash between Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri in the sprint race in Singapore left, in Norris' words, "no-one very happy" at McLaren.

Norris went for a gap at Turn Five on the final lap. It was a legitimate move, in terms of the racing guidelines, but he tried to back out of it as he saw he was not being left sufficient space, and the two cars collided.

Both spun, Piastri into the barriers and retirement and Norris down from fifth place to eighth. What would have been nine points for the team from the sprint therefore became one.

There are two ways of looking at the move.

On a pure competitive level, between two rivals, Norris had the right to go for the move, and he complied with the driving-standards guidelines as to how far alongside he needed to be up to the point he started to back out.

But from a team perspective, it was all risk and no reward.

If Norris had pulled off the move, it would have meant one more point for him and one fewer for Piastri, but for the team collectively it would have made no difference.

What was interesting was that, despite having had initial talks with the team about it after the sprint, Norris was still pushing his point of view after qualifying.

"Really, it's still my fault," he said, "but I deserved to go for the space and I still believe I had the right for it."

That raised a few eyebrows, but the truth is both drivers could have handled themselves better.

While there is an argument Norris should not have tried the move, there is an equally powerful one that, once he had, Piastri should have given him more space, and carried the fight down the following straight.

Team boss Andrea Stella was asked later that evening whether he was concerned about the message about team play not getting through to his drivers, and he dealt with it with his usual diplomacy.

Stella maintained his usual calm, even demeanour, but words like "unacceptable", "disappointed" and "serious" made it abundantly clear how angry he was.

The following day, Norris had changed his tune. Not only did he offer to help out Piastri late in the race as the Australian was trying to pass Lewis Hamilton's fading Ferrari, but he also finally took full responsibility for the incident.

"I can't attempt what I did," he said. "I should never have attempted it in the first place, even if the move was on. I've simply got to think more of the team that I represent rather than myself. It was a mistake on my part and I let down the team."

Stella made it clear McLaren would not deviate from their policy of fairness and equal status between the drivers, even though he is well aware it will lead to issues such as this that test its limits from time to time.

"I classified it as unacceptable," he said, "which is a statement that comes from the team principal, but I was very encouraged by the fact that it's a statement that very rapidly came from our drivers as well.

"So we are aligned as to how we want to lead this team forward in a joint effort between the team and the drivers. The conversations that we are having, they are not finished, but it's not because we need to go back discussing if Lando was alongside Oscar. That's not the interesting bit.

"For me, the interesting bit is a reflection that all the stakeholders - the team, the drivers - will have to make around leading together the team, embracing constantly from inside the cockpit the interest of the team as something that is superior to any particular, singular, individual interest.

"And while the conversations from this point of view are not concluded, and there's more we can do to become a more united and even stronger team, I'm pleased that Lando at some stage in the race adopted this way of thinking.

"This is what I expect as a team principal, this is what the 1,000 people that work at McLaren expect from our drivers."

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993

Verstappen dominates for first Singapore Grand Prix win

Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Antonelli moves to brink of title

I am regularly baffled by teams' tyre strategies, but Ferrari's in Singapore was the worst in recent years. We know Lewis Hamilton is taking responsibility, fair enough, but it wasn't his decision to stay behind Charles Leclerc. Where does this sort of thinking come from? - Julie

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur was especially sensitive about this topic after the race in Singapore, and it led to a particularly awkward news conference as reporters tried to get to the bottom of what had happened, and Vasseur kept cutting them off before they could finish questions.

You could see how hard Vasseur was trying to keep himself calm, and it's easy to understand his feelings.

The past few weeks, after all, have been a trying period for the team with lots of speculation about the future, which led to an unusual intervention from Ferrari after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix to make it clear Vasseur had the full support of chairman John Elkann.

In this case, though, while the strategy certainly looked bizarre from the outside during the race, the explanation was pretty straightforward.

Hamilton was on the back foot from the moment it became clear the medium tyres he was on for the first stint were the wrong ones for this race. The softs were much better.…

title: BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead
author: Anna Tims
text:
It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice

I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments.

Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not.

Since then, I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work.

I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness.

You have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit.

You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged.

It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July.

You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way.

A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September.

The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600.

I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss.

You have the option of a complaint to the Communications Ombudsman but have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record.

Always keep a timeline of interactions with a company and follow up unaddressed complaints promptly and in writing.

title: Is Man Utd's Fernandes issue a symptom or reason for their form?
text:
It is only seven weeks since Bruno Fernandes stood in the Manchester Opera House and spoke of his pride at being named PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26.

The Manchester United captain had already won the Premier League and Football Writers' versions, in recognition of the phenomenal contribution to his side's unexpected third-place finish.

Fernandes scored nine goals and claimed 21 assists, breaking a Premier League record jointly held by Thierry Henry and Kevin de Bruyne.

Over the final 11 games of last season, of the 21 goals United scored, Fernandes either found the net himself or created 12 of them. In the seven-game run that swept United back into Europe's elite club competition after a two-year absence, the 31-year-old was a central figure in nine out of 12 goals.

Statistically, it was remarkable, reminiscent of Eric Cantona in the 1995-96 title-winning campaign when he scored in six successive games, five of them when United only scored once.

"It was a special season for me," Fernandes told an appreciative audience. "I am very proud.

"But we don't play tennis. We don't play just for ourselves. We play for a team, we play for a club, we play for the fans. There is nothing more special than that."

Those words have particular resonance now because, compared with those exceptional statistics, there are some far less impressive ones this season.

Fernandes has played for every minute of Manchester United 's six Premier League games. He has three goals and one assist, all of which came against Ipswich, the second game of the campaign and, so far, his side's only win.

The numbers are actually better than last term, when he scored twice in the opening six games and failed to create any.

However, at that point, Fernandes was playing in the deeper midfield role Ruben Amorim preferred.

While this season is Fernandes' second highest for actual shots, at an average of 3.3 per game - his best was 3.5 in 2020-21 - it is his joint-second lowest for shots on target, at an average of 0.8. His chance creation (2.5 per game on average) is also the second lowest of his time at Old Trafford and down significantly on the 4.0 he returned last season.

Even more startlingly, he has created just one 'big chance' so far this season, the lofted pass that sent Bryan Mbeumo running clear of the Ipswich defence on 30 August. Fernandes' average last season was one per game.

A combination of Fernandes' numbers and his general involvement perhaps goes some way to explaining why United have collected just six points from their opening six games, their worst start to a league campaign in 40 years, when Ron Atkinson was eventually sacked to make way for Sir Alex Ferguson.

But is Fernandes a reason for, or a symptom of, United's malaise?

There is uncertainty over the Portugal playmaker's fitness. Fernandes rarely misses a game but was left out of the recent Nations League encounter with Norway as national team boss Jorge Jesus said the former Sporting man was "playing through pain".

However, Fernandes was fit enough to return for the final two internationals of the extended break. Prior to that, he completed the full 90 minutes in the 4-0 win against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League.

United manager Michael Carrick does not view it as an issue as he prepares his side to face Atletico Madrid on Tuesday.

"He was carrying something but that happens a lot," Carrick said. "Players play with issues.

"It's not ideal but it is manageable. Bruno is able to play. That is the commitment he has got.

"He is pretty much over it, was really bright in training this morning and is looking forward to the game."

Towards the end of last season, when Fernandes' contribution was at its most prolific, Benjamin Sesko was a regular in the number nine role, while veteran Brazilian Casemiro was the anchor in United's midfield.

Of the nine league goals Sesko has scored in 2026, Fernandes created four. Fernandes was responsible for setting up four of the final five goals Casemiro scored as a Manchester United player from 1 February onwards.

Quite aside from goals, it is also clear the presence of Sesko and Casemiro is being missed.

Even Casemiro's biggest admirers could not claim United's current low running stats are because the 34-year-old left for Inter Miami in the summer. However, his positioning and game knowledge remain of a high standard. Fernandes could take risks in the belief United would not be overrun on transition if he lost the ball.

As for Sesko, his fresh shin injury merely extends a lack of involvement which is being keenly felt and for which, as yet, there is no end date.

The club's power brokers ignored a clamour to bring in more striking support in the summer and instead reinforced Carrick's midfield.

But a plan to cover the Slovenian's initial absence by using Mbeumo as a number nine had to be scrapped when Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury just before the opening game at Hull.

Matheus Cunha was given the job instead, but he repeatedly dropped deep, right into the space Fernandes was occupying, and the pair never really found an effective way of dealing with it.

For Fernandes, it feels restrictive, and while he is not a player who lacks confidence, it does seem his decision-making is being affected.

Against Tottenham at the weekend, it took Fernandes an incredible 23 minutes just to complete a pass.

Carrick said on Monday, as he looked ahead to the Champions League meeting with Atletico, that no-one was "guaranteed" a place in his team - but put enough caveats around it to indicate leaving out his captain is not in his thinking.

However, United must start to improve and, that means Fernandes must do the same.

"He's a top player, Bruno," Carrick said.

"Sometimes things don't quite go for you. Sometimes you have a spell of that.

"But he's done some incredible things for this football club and he will do the same in the future, there's no doubt about that."…
